description: The 100-watt Super Lead behind most British rock — almost clean at low volume, and a roar once the power section is working.
The 50-watt Plexi. Same voice as its bigger brother but it breaks up sooner, which is why it turns up on more records than the 100.
Eddie Van Halen's last amp design — a tighter, more modern take on the 5150 he made famous, with the low end kept under control.
Built for a bass and adopted by guitarists instead. The tweed Bassman is where the Marshall sound came from, and it still does blues better than anything.

basedOn: Dweezil Zappa's 1965 blackface Fender Bassman, AB165
description: The blackface Bassman — cleaner and stiffer than the tweed, with the scooped mids Fender moved to in the sixties.
A five-watt one-knob Champ. Too small for a stage and perfect in front of a microphone, which is why so many famous solos were cut on one.

basedOn: Fender Narrow Panel high-powered Tweed Twin, 5F8
description: The high-powered tweed Twin — the loudest thing Fender built before the blackface era, and it stays thick rather than getting brittle.
Brown-panel Fender: the halfway house between tweed warmth and blackface clarity, with the tremolo that era is loved for.
A brown-panel four-by-ten. Loud, round, and famously hard to make sound bad — a clean platform with a little hair on top.
A modern boutique take on the AC30 idea, built to get the chime at a volume that does not clear the room.
German high gain — very tight, very controlled, and voiced for fast picking to stay separated rather than turning to mush.
PRS's modern high-gain amp. Clean and lead voices a long way apart, with a tight bottom end aimed at drop tunings.
A blackface Bandmaster. The same circuit family as the Deluxe Reverb without the reverb, so the top end stays dry and direct.
Bogner's rack preamp — the Ecstasy family's voices in a box that lived in the racks of late-eighties session players.
The JCM800: bright, mid-forward, and tight. Most eighties rock and a good deal of the metal after it went through one of these.

basedOn: Marshall Studio Classic SC20, a 20-watt JCM800
description: A 20-watt JCM800. The same voice at a volume that works in a room with a ceiling.
Slash's signature Marshall, aimed at the sound of the first Guns N' Roses record — a hot-rodded Plexi with more gain than the original had.
The same Slash-voiced Marshall, taken from its cleaner side.
The JTM45 — Marshall's first amp, and still close enough to the tweed Bassman it was copied from to sound like one.

A modern four-channel Marshall that covers the whole history of the brand, from clean to more gain than a Plexi ever had.

Four channels, three voices each, which is the whole point of it: twelve settings that walk from a JTM 45 up to something with more gain than any Marshall sold before it. The models here are the two overdrive channels.

They have a lot of gain on tap. Start with Input Drive lower than feels right and come up — this is an amp that will happily give you more than the song wants.
The JMP-1 preamp, which lived in a rack with a power amp under it. The sound of a lot of early-nineties rock records.
The Silver Jubilee — a Marshall with a diode-clipped gain stage that gives it a slightly compressed, vocal quality all its own.
A small class-A boutique combo — warm, compressed, and happiest overdriven.
The CAA 3+ preamp — a rack unit with a famous clean and a very usable high-gain channel, from the era when everyone played racks.
A boutique American combo built around the blackface Fender idea, with more headroom and better reverb than the original.
Orange's hand-wired 30-watter. Thick and woody rather than bright, with a midrange that sits over a band instead of under it.
Orange's big valve bass head — round, warm, and happy to be pushed until the low end starts to move.
A modern Orange with real gain on tap. Keeps the thick midrange and adds enough saturation for heavy music.
The Tiny Terror. Fifteen watts, two knobs and a tone control — famous for being far louder and nastier than it looks.
An AC15 with Top Boost. The chime of the bigger Vox at a volume you can actually use, and it breaks up early.
The AC30 without Top Boost — darker and rounder than the version most people picture, and the sound of the early British invasion.
The AC30 Top Boost: the jangle. Chimey and bright, and it compresses in a way no Fender does.
A Trainwreck-inspired boutique amp — touch sensitive to the point of being demanding, and enormous when you dig in.
A boutique amp in the Trainwreck tradition, with more headroom than the Komet 60 and the same touch response.
A British boutique high-gain head — tight and aggressive, with a hard-edged midrange.
Diezel's VH4 — German high gain built for tightness above everything, with a low end that stays defined under heavy distortion.
A brown-panel Deluxe. Small, warm, and it starts to break up early, which is most of the appeal.
The 5E3 Tweed Deluxe — two controls that fight each other, almost no headroom, and a raggedness people spend a lot of money to get.
The Deluxe Reverb: the studio clean amp. Loud enough for a small stage, with the reverb and tremolo everyone copies.
Friedman's lower-gain amp — a hot-rodded British voice aimed at classic rock rather than metal.
A small boutique combo built for touch response — clean to crunch on the guitar's volume knob rather than a footswitch.
A boutique amp with a British flavour and boutique headroom — clean, then progressively rude, without ever getting fizzy.
The Diezel VH4 taken from another of its channels — the same tight, modern German high gain.
The Twin Reverb. Loud, clean, and hard to overdrive, which is exactly why it is the reference clean amp for pedals.

basedOn: Dweezil Zappa's modded 1965 blackface Fender Bassman, AB165
description: A modified blackface Bassman — more gain than the original, but still the stiff, clean-edged Fender bottom end.
Engl's Powerball — aggressive, modern and scooped, built squarely for heavy music.
The Bogner Ecstasy — a boutique British-voiced amp that covers Plexi warmth through to modern gain without changing character.
The Uberschall. Bogner's heavy amp: enormous low end and a midrange voiced to cut through it.
A Dumble-style overdrive amp made in numbers. Smooth, singing lead sounds with a clean that stays out of the way.
The BE-100 — a modded Marshall made into a product. Tight, saturated and famously good at rhythm playing.

basedOn: Friedman BE-100, HBE (hot British eq) channel
description: The BE-100's hotter channel, with more gain and a fatter midrange than the standard voice.
Friedman's Plexi-flavoured amp — less gain than the BE and more of the old Marshall bark.
A modern high-gain amp with unusually good clean headroom, so the distortion stays tight rather than woolly.
A small sixties Gibson combo — dark, loose and characterful, nothing like a Fender of the same size.
The Diezel Herbert — more midrange and more personality than the VH4, with a famously useful mid-cut control.
The Hiwatt DR103. Huge clean headroom and a very flat, honest response — the loud amp that stays clean.
A boutique British-voiced amp with more gain than a Vox and more chime than a Marshall.
Marshall's JMP-1 rack preamp — the sound of a lot of early-nineties guitar, and still a very usable clean.
The Blues Junior. A small, cheap, honest Fender combo that breaks up early and has been on more pub stages than anything else.

basedOn: Marshall JVM410HJS, Joe Satriani's signature amp
description: Joe Satriani's JVM — the Marshall platform voiced for sustained lead playing.
The Roland JC-120. Solid state, relentlessly clean, and the chorus built into it is the sound of a lot of eighties records.

basedOn: Carvin Legacy VL100, Steve Vai's signature amp
description: Steve Vai's Carvin signature — a high-gain amp built for smooth sustain rather than aggression.
A hand-wired boutique amp in the British class-A tradition, with more headroom than a Vox.
The Matchless DC-30 — two very different channels, huge chime, and the amp that started the boutique era.
A Dr. Z with an American voice — more Fender than Vox, with plenty of clean before it goes.
An eight-watt Dr. Z. Small enough to overdrive in a bedroom and still sound like a real amp.
The Maz 38 — a boutique amp with a bright, cutting top end and the headroom to stay clean with a band.
A small Swart combo famous for its built-in tube reverb and tremolo — dark, atmospheric, and lovely quiet.
The Dumble Overdrive Special. The most mythologised amp ever built: a glassy clean and a lead voice that sings without getting harsh.
The block-letter 5150 — Eddie Van Halen's amp, and then the amp every nu-metal and hardcore band used. Raw, loud, and unsubtle.
The 6505+, the second-generation 5150. Tighter and a little more refined than the block-letter, and still a rhythm machine.
The Super Lead in its most famous form. Everything about the sound of loud British rock starts here.

basedOn: Marshall Studio Vintage SV20, a 20-watt Plexi
description: A 20-watt Plexi. The same amp at a volume that does not require a stage.
A small Fender with no reverb — quiet, warm, and very easy to record.
The blackface Princeton Reverb. The small studio amp: it breaks up at a usable volume and the reverb is the good one.
The two-channel Dual Rectifier — loose, huge and scooped. The sound of nineties heavy music.
The three-channel Rectifier. Tighter and more controlled than the original, with more usable clean.
A modern Canadian high-gain amp built for tight, articulate metal rhythm playing.
The Ampeg SVT — the loud bass amp. Round and warm clean, and it growls beautifully when pushed.
Bogner's Shiva — a mid-gain amp with a rich, complex clean and an overdrive that never sounds sterile.
A Soldano rack preamp with the SLO voice, for a rig built around a separate power amp.
The later Soldano preamp — the same lineage with more control over the gain structure.
The Soldano SLO-100. The high-gain amp: smooth, singing, and the blueprint nearly every boutique hot-rod followed.
A modern hot-rodded Marshall type with more gain than Marshall ever shipped, and the tightness to use it.
The same Marshall-derived platform from its higher-gain side — aggressive and tight.
An 18-watt British-voiced amp with a power-scaling control, so it sounds cranked at any volume.
The bigger Badger — the same idea with the headroom to stay clean with a drummer.
The blackface Super Reverb. Four ten-inch speakers, a huge clean, and the blues amp of choice for a lot of players.
A sixties Supro — small, gritty, and nothing like a Fender. Jimmy Page's early studio sound.
A modern Supro. Keeps the old raggedness and adds enough volume to use it with a band.
Mesa's Lone Star. A clean Fender-style amp by Mesa standards, with the build quality and a proper lead channel behind it.
An early Dual Rectifier, before the revisions — looser and more open than the ones that followed, and much loved for it.
A blackface Tremolux. A small Fender with the tremolo rather than the reverb, and it overdrives sooner than a Deluxe.
A modern Mesa. Much tighter and more contemporary than a Rectifier, aimed at players who found those too loose.
A Two-Rock — Dumble-inspired, beautifully clean, and built to be the platform a pedalboard sits in front of.
Mesa's big valve bass head — clean, punchy, and with far more control than most bass amps of its era.

basedOn: Mesa/Boogie JP-2C, the John Petrucci Mark IIC+
description: John Petrucci's Mark IIC+, made again as a product. The classic Mesa lead voice with modern tightness.
The Mark IIC+: the most sought-after Mesa ever built. Compressed, midrange-heavy lead sounds and the amp behind a lot of eighties metal.
A modified Mark IIC+, pushed further than the factory took it.
The Mark IV — a Mark with three real channels, and the graphic EQ that makes the family's sound what it is.
The Mark V. Every Mark voice in one amp, with the tightness of the modern ones.
A small Mesa combo, voiced far cleaner and more American than the Marks — easy to like and easy to record.
The Mesa TriAxis — the Mark preamp voices in a rack unit, and the sound of a lot of nineties studio guitar.
A custom Fender built around the old tweed and brown voices, with a proper valve tremolo.
A brown-panel Vibrolux. Small, warm, and the tremolo is the reason to reach for it.
The Vibroverb — a blackface Fender with a fifteen-inch speaker, so the low end is looser and rounder than a Deluxe.
A Trainwreck Express. Ferociously touch-sensitive, no master volume, and it rewards playing harder more than any other amp here.
The Vox-flavoured Trainwreck — chime and bite, and the same demanding responsiveness.
The Trainwreck with the most gain of the three, and still entirely controlled from the guitar.
